questions.question: When does Git trigger a merge conflict?

options.A: Whenever any two branches are merged
options.B: When competing changes are made to the same line of a file, or when a file is deleted in one branch and edited in another
options.C: Only when your internet connection drops during merge

questions.explanation: If changes occur in different files or different lines, Git merges automatically. Conflicts only happen when Git cannot mathematically determine which change should take precedence.

questions.question: In a Git conflict marker, what does the section between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` represent?

options.A: Changes from the incoming branch you are trying to merge
options.B: Changes on the current active branch you are currently on
options.D: Syntax errors detected by the compiler

questions.explanation: `<<<<<<< HEAD` marks the start of changes on your current receiving branch (`HEAD`). `=======` is the dividing center line.

questions.question: In a Git conflict marker, what does the section between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature-branch` represent?

options.A: Changes from the incoming branch being merged into your current branch
options.B: Deleted files from the trash bin

questions.explanation: The bottom half shows the incoming changes from the branch you are attempting to merge.

questions.question: Which command completely cancels a conflicted merge and restores the repository to its pre-merge state?
questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` restores the branch state to before `git merge` was executed, giving you a clean slate.

questions.question: After manually editing a conflicted file to remove conflict markers and select the correct code, what must you do next?

options.B: Stage the resolved file with `git add <file>` and run `git commit` to finalize the merge commit

questions.explanation: Staging the file signals to Git that the conflict in that file has been resolved. `git commit` finishes the merge.

questions.question: What does VS Code's 'Accept Current Change' option choose during a merge conflict?

options.A: Keeps the code from your currently checked-out branch (`HEAD`) and discards the incoming branch's changes
options.B: Keeps the incoming changes from the other branch

questions.explanation: 'Current change' refers to your active branch (`HEAD`).

questions.question: What happens if a developer accidentally commits conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`) to their code?

options.A: Git automatically fixes them during push
options.B: The conflict markers will be saved into the file as literal text, usually causing syntax errors or build failures in the application
options.D: The file is converted to a PDF

questions.explanation: Git markers are plain text. If not cleaned up, they remain in the source code and break compilation/runtime.

questions.question: If Alice and Bob edit completely different files in the same repository, will a merge conflict occur?

options.A: Yes, Git always conflicts when two people work at the same time
options.B: No, Git will automatically combine changes from different files without conflict
options.C: Only if they use the same operating system

questions.explanation: Git cleanly auto-merges changes in different files or even different sections of the same file.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best proactive way to minimize merge conflicts in a team?

options.A: Only allow one person to commit per week
options.B: Keep feature branches small, pull from `main` frequently, and communicate with teammates about who is touching shared files

questions.explanation: Small, short-lived branches combined with daily `git pull` drastically reduce divergence and conflicts.

questions.question: Which command shows exactly which files currently have unresolved merge conflicts?
questions.explanation: `git status` highlights unmerged paths under 'Unmerged paths:' (e.g. `both modified: hello.txt`).
